social_title: The September Pick: Mr. Market Took $23B Off This Bank For $300M Of Fees
subtitle: Mr. Market is arguing about this bank’s earnings. The number that moves 90% of the answer is the one nobody is defending, so I rebuilt it from the company’s own capital stack, and it changed the call.
title: The September Pick: Mr. Market Took $23B Off This Bank For $300M Of Fees
description: Mr. Market is arguing about this bank’s earnings. The number that moves 90% of the answer is the one nobody is defending, so I rebuilt it from the company’s own capital stack, and it changed the call.
body_html:
Usually I don’t go to networking events, and now even less than I used to. But in July I went to an informal CFA Toronto gathering for drinks. I had a nice time and ended up chatting with a portfolio manager focused on US financials.

I asked for his top pick; it was WFC. I asked him why, and he gave me his elevator pitch. In his pitch he was comparing all the US large-cap financials on the same metric, but I knew that one of those companies wasn’t really comparable because of what sits in its capital structure. I asked him about it, and he brushed off my question with an ambiguous non-answer that sounded smart.

Anyways, I kept thinking about it, as this company has been staring at me for months on my screener, so I took a deeper look and lo and behold…it became the September Stock Pick.

That capital structure question turned out to be the whole thesis. Every valuation has one input that does most of the work, and it is almost never the one people argue about.

I ran 100,000 simulations on this month’s pick, and then I looked at which assumption was actually moving the output. Nine of every ten dollars of dispersion came from a single number: the rate I use to discount the company’s future profits back to today. The earnings path, the payout, the growth rate, the terminal assumption, all of them together accounted for the rest.

So I went looking for who else was making this argument, and the answer is nobody. Mr. Market is valuing this bank on a multiple of next year’s earnings, on a chart, on a quant score. Where a discount rate does get named, it arrives asserted, with no beta, no build-up and no justification of any kind, and then the argument moves straight back to the earnings forecast.

I have been skeptical of the megabanks for years, for the reason McKinsey put plainly in this year’s Global Banking Annual Review: banking carries the lowest price-to-book and price-to-earnings ratios of any industry on earth, and it has for a very long time. Millions of people pricing an industry that low for that long is a verdict about required returns. The question I set out to answer this month is whether that verdict applies to this particular bank, and my answer is that it does not.

First I will explain what the business actually does and where the earnings come from. Then I will walk through the engine that I think the market is underrating, which is mechanical rather than cyclical and runs for five more years. Then we will do the real work on the discount rate, three different ways, and check it against what the company’s own capital stack is telling us. Finally I will put the whole thing through the model, steel-man the case against me, and give you the number.

So earlier today, I sent an email to paid subscribers with the trade alert.

I bought BAC shares representing 3.5% of the portfolio and I closed SYF locking a 52% gain.

And financed the gap by trimming a bit more from DELL.

Later next week, I will be sending a post-mortem on SYF.

Contents

  • The company

  • TLDR

  • How the stock ranks

  • What this business actually is, in plain language

  • The repricing engine: five years of contracted earnings growth

  • The fee franchise, and the honest problem with it

  • Operating leverage, and what 114 live AI applications are worth

  • The number that moves everything: a real look at the cost of equity

  • A note on the securities one rung up

  • The model, the target, and what has to be true

  • The Monte Carlo: 100,000 runs

  • Steel-manning the case against me

  • Verdict

The company

BAC trades at $59 as I write, which puts it at 1.6x book value and 2.0x tangible book.

Until this morning it sat within a couple of dollars of its all-time high, having climbed steadily off the February lows.

That changed at a financial services conference last week, where the CEO guided third-quarter investment banking fees to $1.6B-$1.8B against $2.0B in the same quarter last year, with consensus sitting near $2.0B, and said sales and trading would be flat. The stock fell more than 5% and pulled the bank index down 2.7% with it.

I am going to use that as the opening exhibit. Investment banking fees were 6.6% of revenue last quarter. The guidance takes about $300M out of one quarter, call it $950M a year after tax if it persists. Mr. Market marked the company down by $23B. That is 24x the annualized change in after-tax earnings, applied to the most cyclical line in the business, in an afternoon.

Either the market learned something profound about this bank’s next decade before lunch, or it repriced a number it has never examined. The rest of this article is about which.

Even after the recent drop, BAC still carries close to the highest premium to book value it has had in a decade. On a pure screen it looks late.

My argument is that the premium to book is the correct output of a bank whose required return has fallen, and that almost nobody has checked whether that is what happened.

TLDR

Revenue grew 15% y/y in Q2 with every segment contributing, and EPS grew 34%. Operating leverage was 6.6%.

  • ROTCE reached 17%, up 342bps y/y, and ROE reached 12.7%, up 259bps.

  • The securities book is repricing from a 2021 world into a 2026 one, and the runway on that is five more years.

  • Industry net interest margins are compressing. BAC’s are expanding, up 13bps y/y excluding Global Markets.

  • Cost of equity moves 90% of the variance in my model. I rebuilt it three ways and cross-checked it against BAC’s own preferred stack, which clears at 6.0%-6.6%.

  • BAC is my September’26 Stock Pick with a fair value of $83, roughly 40%.

  • The preferreds deserve their own look, and I explain why below.

How the stock ranks

BAC scores 81 on RankedStocks.com, which puts it in the Elite band, and the score has climbed 6.5 points in the last week. Against the 1,081 US financials in the database it sits in the 90th percentile globally…

… and the 91st among its own country peers.

Profitability 94. Cash from operations and cash per share carry this factor. The return metrics are the weaker half, with trailing ROE and return on total assets both scoring below the midpoint. That split is the thesis in miniature. BAC generates enormous absolute cash and has historically converted it into mediocre returns on the equity backing it. Q2 annualized at 12.7% on common equity against the 11.6% trailing figure in the table, so the return metrics are catching up to the cash metrics, and the factor is scoring a bank that has already changed.

Valuation 35. The earnings multiples are bringing the score down, with forward P/E and P/B both scoring in the thirties. P/CF scores 80, which is the same tension the Profitability factor shows: cheap against the cash, expensive against the book. A reader who stops at the headline 35 concludes the stock is expensive. A reader who opens the breakdown learns that the market is paying up for BAC’s equity and paying very little for its cash generation, which is a more interesting fact and one I will come back to.

Growth 62. Every paired metric in the table scores better on the trailing column than on the forward one.

The forward column is consensus, and consensus for this name has been wrong in the same direction for a while. BAC has beaten on EPS in 105 of its last 123 reports.

Sentiment 84 and Outlook 73. Both reflect a stock that has re-rated hard and a consensus that has been chasing it upward. The Street’s target sits at $66 against 54 analysts, which is 11% above this morning’s price and well below my number.

You can run this same screen on any ticker at RankedStocks.com, and it costs nothing.

What this business actually is, in plain language

A bank makes money two ways, and the difference matters enormously for how you value one.

The first is the spread. BAC holds $2.0T of customer deposits and pays an average of 1.46% for them. It lends and invests that money at a higher rate, and the gap is net interest income. In Q2 that was $16.0B, which is roughly half the company’s revenue. The width of the gap is the net interest yield, and BAC’s was 2.08%, or 2.57% if you strip out the trading business, whose balance sheet distorts the ratio.

The second is fees. Wealth management charges a percentage of client assets. Investment banking charges for deals. Trading earns a spread on client flow. Card and service charges arrive monthly. This is roughly the other half of revenue, it consumes very little capital, and it is worth more per dollar than spread income because it does not require a balance sheet to produce.

The metric that ties it together is return on tangible common equity, ROTCE. Take the profit that belongs to ordinary shareholders, divide by the equity backing it after stripping out goodwill, and you have the number that decides whether a bank is worth more or less than its book value. Above the cost of equity, the bank creates value and should trade at a premium to book. Below it, the bank destroys value and should trade at a discount. That is not a rule of thumb, it is arithmetic, and it is why the cost of equity is the number this whole article turns on.

Every one of those returns moved higher in the second quarter, and by a lot.

Four businesses produced it, and the striking thing is that all four grew loans, deposits, revenue and net income in the same quarter, with positive operating leverage in each. That is rarer than it sounds. Consumer Banking and wealth management earn the highest returns on the capital allocated to them, and Global Banking the lowest.

The repricing engine: five years of contracted earnings growth

In 2020 and 2021, deposits flooded into the banking system and there was nothing to do with them. Short-term instruments paid nothing. BAC took a large share of that money and bought long-dated mortgage-backed securities and Treasuries, locking in yields of 2.1% and 1.4%. Then rates went up, and BAC was left holding more low-yielding paper than any of its peers. It was the single most criticized decision of the CEO’s tenure and it cost the bank several years of earnings power.

Here is what changed.

Those securities mature. When they do, the cash comes back at par and gets reinvested at today’s rates, and the difference drops straight into net interest income. The held-to-maturity book stood at $541B a year ago. It ended Q2 at $506B. That is $35B that has already rolled from a 2021 world into a 2026 one.

The pace from here is $12B-$15B a quarter of mortgage-backed securities and mortgage loans, reinvested 150bps-200bps higher, and the company has been explicit that this runs for about five more years at current rates rather than for a few quarters. Separately, roughly $100B of expensive short-term wholesale funding is being paid down as deposits fund more of the balance sheet, which helps the yield rather than the income, and frees capital that lifts ROTCE.

The temptation here is to over-attribute, so run the arithmetic.

The disclosed roll-off creates something like $25M-$30M of new annualized net interest income each quarter, compounding. Meaningful, and nowhere near enough on its own to explain 9% growth on a $60B base. Loan growth of 8%, deposit growth, funding paydown and mix are doing most of the heavy lifting. What the repricing gives you is something better than size: it is contractual, and it happens whether or not the economy cooperates, as long as rates stay somewhere near here.

Now the part that turned this from a nice mechanic into a September pick. The rest of the banking system is going the other way. The St. Louis Fed reported in June that the industry’s net interest margin fell to 3.22% in the first quarter from 3.30%, with loan yields dropping from 6.75% to 6.51% and the system posting its first quarterly decline in net interest income since mid-2024. Loan yields are falling faster than funding costs.

BAC’s went the other way, from 2.44% to 2.57% excluding Global Markets, because BAC is the bank with the most legacy paper still left to reprice. The duration mistake that punished it through the hiking cycle is the reason its margin is expanding while the industry’s compresses. So the thing that made BAC the worst-positioned megabank in 2022 is the thing that makes it the best-positioned one now, and Mr. Market has spent three years learning to think of BAC as the bank with the bond problem.

Funding helps too. The blended deposit rate paid has fallen every quarter for a year, and the consumer book costs BAC under half a percent. Low-interest and noninterest-bearing checking grew 3%, so the cheap, sticky, retail money is growing faster than the expensive kind.

The fee franchise, and the honest problem with it

Half of BAC’s revenue does not depend on rates at all, and in Q2 that half grew faster than the spread half. Sales and trading rose 33%, investment banking fees rose 50%, and asset management fees rose 20%.

The problem is obvious, and every bull writing about this name concedes it. Consolidated revenue grew 15%, and Consumer Banking, the largest and steadiest segment, grew revenue 4.8%. The 15% was carried by the two businesses that are hostage to market conditions. Equities revenue up 70% in a quarter is not a run rate, it is a quarter.

So here is the argument that survives the concession.

Strip capital markets back to something normal and BAC is a mid-single-digit revenue grower.

Fine.

The useful question is the level of the fee base underneath the trading line rather than its growth rate, and the character of that base has changed. Global Wealth and Investment Management is the clearest case. Its earnings are a percentage of $4.9T of client balances; asset management fees grew 20%, and the segment’s net income grew 42% to a 26% return on allocated capital. That is an annuity linked to asset values. It reprices with markets rather than with the deal calendar, and it is being valued today inside a 13.4x bank multiple.

The same is partly true of Global Markets, where prime brokerage and equities financing balances earn a spread on client positions that persists whether or not volumes spike. That is a minority of the increase and the trading line is genuinely cyclical. But the level is structurally higher than it was five years ago, and Mr. Market is capitalizing it as though the entire increase is a spike.

Operating leverage, and what 114 live AI applications are worth

The efficiency ratio, which is expense divided by revenue, has fallen four percentage points in a year, and expenses grew at roughly half the rate of revenue.

Expense growth has been the standing complaint against BAC for four years. Costs rose fast through the post-pandemic period while the technology platforms were being built. The argument now is that those platforms have moved from construction to maintenance, which should mean a permanently lower rate of expense growth.

A third of the live generative applications are fully deployed, the developer population reports productivity gains above 20%, and more than 20,000 wealth professionals are using it to expand the number of clients each one can serve. That last one is the interesting number, because advisor capacity is the binding constraint on the highest-return business BAC owns.

I am wary of counting this as earnings; the claim I will defend is narrower. If BAC holds 300bps-400bps of operating leverage for another two years, the efficiency ratio goes to the low 50s, and the terminal ROTCE the market is carrying for this bank is too low. The efficiency ratio is the input that determines the terminal return, and it is the input the AI programme most directly attacks.

The number that moves everything: a real look at the cost of equity

Now the centre of the article.

The cost of equity is the annual return a shareholder must expect in order to be willing to own the stock rather than something safer. A lower rate makes distant profits worth more today.

I ran the model 100,000 times, sampling every uncertain input from its own distribution, and then decomposed the variance in the output.

Terminal ROTCE, the input the whole debate is about, is the second bar and it is a fraction of the first. The payout ratio barely registers. If you want to argue about what BAC is worth, this chart says you should be arguing about the discount rate.

My model uses a cost of equity of 8.4%, built the standard way: a risk-free rate of 4.80%, plus a beta of 0.86, times an equity risk premium of 4.23%.

Two of those three are not controversial and I will deal with them quickly. The risk-free rate of 4.8% is the 10-year Treasury, which the Federal Reserve’s H.15 release put at 4.8% on 9 September. The equity risk premium of 4.23% is ’s implied premium for the S&P 500, computed from actual index cash flows rather than from historical averages, and published in his dataset. Both are current and both are sourced from the primary publisher.

The beta is the whole argument, so let me show you the three honest ways to get one and what each produces.

Method one: the bottom-up sector beta

Damodaran’s own recommendation, for the specific reason that a regression on a single company is statistically noisy, is to take the average beta of the industry and re-lever it to the company’s own capital structure. His money-centre banking group carries an unlevered, cash-adjusted beta of 0.44. Re-levered to BAC, that lands in the low-to-mid 0.8s and produces a cost of equity around 8.4%.

Method two: the regression

Three years of returns against the S&P 500, using the Fed’s own index series. Weekly returns give a beta of 1.15. Monthly returns give 1.12. Applying the Blume adjustment, which pulls estimated betas toward one because they historically drift that way, gives 1.10.

Two commercial data providers publish 1.16 and 1.13. So the regression family clusters between 1.10 and 1.16, and produces a cost of equity between 9.4% and 9.7%.

That is a 130bps spread between two defensible methods, and on this model 130bps is worth roughly $19 a share. So the entire question of whether BAC is a buy comes down to which beta you believe, and I do not think you can settle that with a third regression.

Method three: ask the market what it charges this company

Which brings me to the thing nobody else has done.

BAC has $25.0B of preferred stock outstanding. Preferred shares sit above the common in the capital structure and below the debt, they pay a fixed dividend forever, and most importantly for our purposes, they trade every day. Their yield is a directly observable market price for permanent, junior, non-maturing capital issued by this specific company against this specific balance sheet.

Here is where they clear:

Common equity sits one rung below that, so it must cost more.

The question is how much more.

At 8.4%, I am saying the common costs about 200bps more than the preferred. At the 10% the bears reach for, the claim is 340bps-400bps more, though it is never stated that way because the preferred never enters the discussion.

I think 200bps is the better estimate for this particular bank. Preferred dividends of $755M in the first half consumed under 5% of after-tax income, so coverage is above twenty times. There is $276B of common equity standing junior to that $25B of preferred, absorbing losses first. The Federal Reserve’s 2026 stress test left BAC’s stress capital buffer at 2.5%, which is the regulatory floor and the best outcome available, and the aggregate capital drawdown across the tested banks improved to 1.6 percentage points from 1.8.

Scale across four segments produces less volatility in profitability than the banking industry generally.

A bank whose junior capital clears at 6.3%, whose regulator says its stressed capital depletion is at the statutory floor, and whose earnings volatility is below its industry, does not have a 10% cost of equity on its common. It has something in the eights.

The sanity check

The honest test of any discount rate is to invert the model and ask what rate the market is currently applying.

There are two ways to do it.

The first is the identity that price-to-book equals ROE minus growth, divided by cost of equity minus growth. BAC now trades at 1.6x book. Solve for the cost of equity at the Q2 return of 12.7% and 2.5% growth, and Mr. Market is discounting at 9.3%. On Friday the same arithmetic gave just under 9%, so this morning moved the required return 35bps in my favour.

The second is to solve the full ten-year model backwards for the rate that reproduces today’s price, which lands between 9.9% and 10.3% depending on which earnings path you feed it. So Mr. Market is now demanding somewhere between 9.3% and 10.3% to own this bank, which is to say it has arrived at the number the bears assert, without ever defending it.

My 8.4% is a long way from that. The precise claim is narrow: Mr. Market is applying a required return appropriate to a bank with average earnings volatility to a bank whose regulator, whose capital stack and whose own segment mix all say it has less. Close that gap and you get $83.

Banking as a sector has the lowest price-to-book of any industry, and global banking return on tangible equity was 11.8% last year, down from 12.4%. BAC earned 17.0%. The sector discount exists because the average bank does not earn its cost of capital. Applying the average bank’s required return to a bank earning 500bps above the sector is the error I think the market is making, and the preferred market is where you can see it most cleanly.

A note on the securities one rung up

I am buying the common. But the analysis above has an obvious implication: if the argument is that BAC’s junior capital is underpriced for its risk, the preferred shares are the purest expression of that view. They yield 6.0%-6.6% against the common’s 2.05%, they sit senior to the $276B of common equity that absorbs losses first, and their coupon is contractual rather than a residual claim on a return that has to keep improving.

Two specifics worth knowing.

The low-coupon series, NN and QQ, yield the most at 6.6% precisely because their coupons are small, which makes it uneconomic for BAC to redeem them. You are paid more and you face less call risk, which is the opposite of how these usually trade.

Series L is the odd one. It is a 7.25% convertible on a $1,000 liquidation preference, it converts into 20 common shares, and it has no call feature at all, so BAC cannot redeem it. Forced conversion triggers if the common trades above $65 for 20 of any 30 trading days, and this morning pushed the common back to $59, so that clock has stopped for now. Series L turned dilutive this year and now adds 62 million shares to the diluted count, with $56M of quarterly dividends added back. That sizes the series at roughly $3.1B. It was antidilutive in the same quarter last year, which tells you how far the stock has moved.

The consequence matters for the common holder. Those 62 million shares are already inside the 7,294 million diluted count my model divides by, so the conversion is priced in. And BAC has a real incentive to force it: twenty common shares pay $25.60 a year at the new dividend, against $72.50 on the preferred. Converting cuts the cash cost of that stack by nearly two thirds and moves $3.1B from preferred into common equity tier 1 capital.

For anyone who wants the return without the requirement that ROTCE keeps climbing, that is where I would look first.

The model, the target, and what has to be true

I value banks with an excess return model at the cost of equity rather than on a multiple of one guided year, which is the method Damodaran sets out in Valuing Financial Service Firms (recommended read if you are into this).

The logic is that for a bank, debt is raw material rather than financing, so FCF to the firm is meaningless, and the only coherent thing to value is the equity directly. The model starts from the common shareholders’ book value, adds the present value of every year in which the bank earns more on that book than shareholders require, and adds a terminal value.

The starting book is the $276B of common shareholders’ equity at 30 June, which excludes the $25B of preferred because that money belongs to someone else.

The base case holds return on common equity at 13.2% for ten years, fading to 12.5% in the terminal year, with a payout of 48% and terminal growth of 2.5%. Against Q2’s actual 12.7%, the 13.2% is a modest step up, and the repricing runway is the reason I am comfortable with it.

That produces $83, about 40% above this morning’s price.

What would have to be true to push it higher, and what would pull it down, anchored to what the model actually assumes:

The cost of equity. The model uses 8.4%. Every 50bps is worth roughly $8 a share. If BAC re-rates toward the required return its own preferred stack implies, that is the entire move. This is the lever, and it is why the article is built around it.

Return on common equity above 13.2%. The model holds it flat for a decade. Q2 annualized at 12.7% and the trend across five quarters runs 10.1%, 11.4%, 10.5%, 12.0%, 12.7%. If the efficiency ratio reaches the low 50s and the repricing lands as scheduled, 14% is reachable, and each point of sustained ROE is worth about $7.

The payout ratio. The model assumes 48%, against a five-year actual of 76.9%. A lower payout raises the value in this framework because retained capital earns above the cost of equity, so this assumption flatters the target. I have left it because BAC’s capital requirements are likely to fall rather than rise under the Basel III re-proposal, which would let it retain less and distribute more, and because the sensitivity is small. Move it to 72% and the value falls to about $75. That is the single most conservative adjustment a skeptical reader can make, and the stock still has upside at it.

The Monte Carlo: 100,000 runs

ROE and payout are correlated at negative 0.4, which stops the simulation producing the impossible combination of very high returns and very high distributions at the same time. The more important one is the cost of equity, which is not sampled around my 8.4%. It is sampled around 9%, with a standard deviation of half a point, which centres the whole exercise on Mr. Market’s number rather than on mine and covers the range the inversion above produced. I am running the simulation against myself.

Run it that way and the shares still clear $62.69, the close the simulation was set against, in 82.8% of the 100,000 trials, and this morning’s price is more than three dollars below that. The median outcome is $73 and the mean is $74, both below my $83, which is exactly what you would expect when the discount rate is deliberately set against the thesis. The fifth percentile is $56 and the ninety-fifth is $96.

The case does not need you to accept 8.4%. Hand the model the cost of equity Mr. Market is using, leave every other assumption where it is, and the shares are still worth more than they cost about five times out of six. The 8.4% argument is what turns a decent outcome into a large one.

If this changed how you think about bank valuations, send it to someone who still values them on a multiple of next year.

Share

Steel-manning the case against me

These are the arguments against me that I found hardest to dismiss. They are ranked, and the first one is the one that would actually cost me money. It also arrived early.

First, the growth is in the wrong segments. Consolidated revenue grew 15% and Consumer Banking grew 4.8%. Equities up 70%, investment banking fees up 50%, sales and trading up 33%. Take capital markets back to a normal year and BAC is a mid-single-digit grower with a 12% return, and my 13.2% assumption starts to look like an extrapolation of a good quarter.

My answer is that the level of the fee base is higher rather than the growth rate being durable, and that GWIM’s asset-linked fees are a different animal from trading. But I hold that view with less confidence than anything else in this article, and if Q3 shows capital markets normalizing while consumer stays at 5%, the thesis is weaker rather than merely delayed. This morning delivered the first instalment of exactly that, with investment banking fees guided down more than 10% and trading flat. One quarter does not settle it, and I would rather the number had come in the other way.

Second, the consumer may be turning. US retail sales fell in July for the first time in nine months. More tellingly, the payment networks have badly lagged the banks this year. American Express [] is down 13%, Mastercard [] is up 1% and Visa [] is up 7%, against 13% for the bank index. If the consumer were accelerating, the networks are the first place it would show.

BAC’s own credit data points the other way: charge-offs improved, criticized commercial exposure fell $5.8B, and nonperforming loans declined. All of that is backward-looking, which is precisely the bear’s point.

Third, the valuation sits near a decade high on every book-based measure. Even after this morning’s fall, BAC is close to the top of its ten-year price-to-book range.

My response is the whole middle of this article, and the risk inside it is simple: if I am wrong about the cost of equity, the premium to book is Mr. Market being generous rather than Mr. Market being right, and the stock is expensive. That is the bet.

Fourth, the rate sensitivity is asymmetric and it is disclosed. A 100bps parallel fall in the curve costs BAC $2.2B of net interest income over twelve months. A 100bps rise adds only $1.0B. The current guidance is built on a forward curve that has moved substantially in BAC’s favour this year, and the same steepening that lifted the guide can reverse. This is the argument that most directly attacks the repricing engine, because reinvestment yields fall with the curve. It is also the argument my method is least exposed to, since valuing the bank on a required return and a mid-cycle return on equity rather than on a rate path is the reason to build the model this way in the first place.

Fifth, the repricing schedule has been described loosely. Management has quantified the roll-off differently at different times; the spread pickup on reinvestment has come down from 200bps-225bps to 150bps-200bps as the front end has fallen, and guidance about which half of 2026 gets more of the benefit has moved between quarters. The tailwind is real and the disclosure around it has not been consistent, so I would treat the five-year runway as a direction rather than a schedule.

And one that is not numbered, because it is a governance point rather than a modelling one. The allowance for loan losses has been slowly shrinking as a share of the book, now 1.08%, while nonperforming loans have held around half a percent. The cushion is adequate and it is thinner than it was. In a benign quarter that is efficient capital use. In the quarter the cycle turns, it is the difference between a reserve release and a reserve build, and reserve builds are how bank quarters go from good to bad without anything happening to the business.

Verdict

BAC is my September Stock Pick a fair value of $83.

So here is the thing to sit with. Investment banking fees will be about $300M lighter this quarter, and Mr. Market took $23B off the company for it. Nobody changed their view of what this bank earns in 2031. The only thing that really moved was the rate at which those earnings get discounted, and that rate has been quoted on the NYSE the whole time, four tickers down from the one everybody was watching.
